messages.body_plain:
On 5/31/13 4:15 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> You need to store rho and the state (at the very least momentum) at the boundary of each subtree -- maybe that scales as log(n)?  I'm pretty sure the code is as tight as it can be without appealing to pools or the like.

Imisread n as the number of leapfrog steps,
not the depth.

Let's switch to the NUTS arXiv paper notation, where
j is tree depth and 2^j the number of leaf nodes (leapfrog
steps are in one-one correspondence with leaf nodes).

Section 3.1.2 of the paper provides a O(j) memory algorithm.  It's a pretty
simple induction that assumes you only store the sample that
would be produced (if any) from each subtree and its (position,momentum)
at the endpoints.   Because NUTS only checks that the ends of
each subtree don't make a U-turn, once you've completed a subtree
and chosen a sample from it, you never need to look inside it again.

Of course, it's still O(2^j) time because we do have to do each
leapfrog step.

If you're using O(j^2) for some reason, that could account
for the increased number of objects you're finding in the profiles.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: merging pull/88?
messages.body_plain:
Was there more context here as to which class I should
be looking at?  I'm just not sure any of this is under
our control.

I also seem to recall there being some differences in
the specs for iterators in C++11 around return-by-reference
and return-by-value:

   https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!topic/comp.std.c++/f0CdiAZAl_Y

You can see that the reference type changed between C++98 and
C++11 here:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/iterator/istreambuf_iterator/

In C++11, it's charT&, whereas in C++98, it was just charT.
I wish they'd have defined operator* more precisely like they
did for everything else.  I'm guessing it may return a reference
type.  So I'm guessing this example:

   charT operator*() const { return sbuf_->sgetc(); }

would be this in C++11:

   charT& operator*() const { return sbuf_->sgetc(); }

which would cause a problem by returning a reference to
a local [namely the return of sbuf_->sgetc()].

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'm looking at it NUTS now.  I'm still trying to figure out
if we can get away from static casting ps points.

To see that memory is O(j) for a depth j tree, just use
a simple induction.

Base step:  You can build a depth 0 tree (single node) in
constant time --- there's nothing to build.

Inductive step:   Suppose you can build a depth n tree in
memory size O(n).  To build a depth (n + 1) tree, you need to
first build a depth n tree for the first half, which will
take O(n) memory.  Then you trim it down to its edges, so you're
now using a constant amount of memory and have maxed out at O(n).
Now build the depth n tree making up the second half of the
depth (n + 1) tree.  That will take O(n) memory.  Adding the
constant memory required to be stored for the first half, we
get O(n + 1) total.

- Bob

On 6/1/13 4:26 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> It's a little more complicated than that: because you're building the tree recursively you have many incomplete trees in memory at any given time.  It's easier to draw than to describe, but in any case it might end up being O(j) and I just made a bad order calculation. > To see that memory is O(j) for a depth j tree, just use
> a simple induction.
>
> Base step:  You can build a depth 0 tree (single node) in
> constant time --- there's nothing to build.
>
> Inductive step:   Suppose you can build a depth n tree in
> memory size O(n).  To build a depth (n + 1) tree, you need to
> first build a depth n tree for the first half, which will
> take O(n) memory.  Then you trim it down to its edges, so you're
> now using a constant amount of memory and have maxed out at O(n).
> Now build the depth n tree making up the second half of the
> depth (n + 1) tree.  That will take O(n) memory.  Adding the
> constant memory required to be stored for the first half, we
> get O(n + 1) total.

Right.  That's what I meant?  :-p

That's why I like having immutable objects.  You guarantee
they're always in a reasonable state.

Setting a default of zero isn't the solution, though.
If you're going to make a mutable class like this, you're
already pushing the burden to do the right thing to the client code.

I'd rather NOT have reasonable "guesses", because they can mask
bigger issues.

Since these constructors don't seem to be called anywhere, they're
just cluttering up the code.

around.  You may be able to reuse them more efficiently.

>> means you wind up allocating another pointer per object
>> for the vtable.
>

It's probably not going to matter here because the class is
going to be relatively large compared to the vtable pointer.
For smaller classes like var, it absolutely matters.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] speeding up ps_point
messages.body_plain:
With the changes in the current feature/fast_constructor branch the timing comparison is better but still not perfect.  We're down to about 25% slowdown, but that starts to disappear when the models become nontrivial (taking more than a few seconds to run) and the gradient computations start to dominate.  I'm guessing the turnover past x=1 is due to the faster agrad computations implemented since v.1.3.0.

We should probably start looking into culling acid test models to better reflect the more computationally complex models people are using.

On Sat, Jun 1, 2013 at 8:51 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Some comments on
>
>   src/stan/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/ps_point.hpp
>
> now that we know it's a bottleneck.
>
> 0.  Are the public member variables manipulated directly?  Otherwise
> I don't see how you could get a ps_point with nonzero values.
>
> If everything's public like this, you can use struct.
>
> 1.  In the constructor, do we really need a zero-init?
>
>    ps_point(int n, int m): q(n), r(m), p(Eigen::VectorXd::Zero(n)),
>                                  V(0), g(Eigen::VectorXd::Zero(n))
>
> This will result in an element-by-element copy from the expression
> template constructed with Zero(n).   If you just start p and g out
> with their size-based constructor, it should be much.  (You may need
> to specify rows and columns to avoid ambiguity in the constructor
> signatures.)  You can always zero these things out later when you
> need to.
>
> 2.  This copy_base function could probably be replaced with a copy
> constructor, and then new instances created rather than existing
> ones copied.
>
>       void copy_base(ps_point& z) {
>         q = z.q;
>         r = z.r;
>         p = z.p;
>         V = z.V;
>         g = z.g;
>       }
>
> I'd rather see things like ps_point be immutable.  (Or if we
> must make them mutable, then share them in a pool!)
>
> If that won't work, then you could speed this up if in fact
> the copy constructor is super-slow compared to resizing and
> copying data.
>
> Also, it'd be nice to have the z reference be const here.  This
> won't work given that the fields are not constant.  You could
> provide const accessos.
>
>
>
> 3.  For these gets:
>
>       virtual void get_param_names(std::vector<std::string>& model_names,
>                                    std::vector<std::string>& names) {
>         for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); ++i)
>           names.push_back(model_names.at <http://model_names.at>(i));
>         for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); ++i)
>           names.push_back(std::string("p_") + model_names.at <http://model_names.at>(i));
>         for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); ++i)
>           names.push_back(std::string("g_") + model_names.at <http://model_names.at>(i));
>       }
>
>       virtual void get_params(std::vector<double>& values) {
>         for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); ++i)
>           values.push_back(q.at <http://q.at>(i));
>         for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); ++i)
>           values.push_back(p(i));
>         for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); ++i)
>           values.push_back(g(i));
>       }
>
> a.  Do they really need to be virtual?  The only reason for this would
> be if you were going to use them when their class isn't known statically.
> Can we get around that somehow, like with the curiously recursive template
> pattern?  If they're virtual, do you want virtual destructors, too?
>
> b.  You can use assign() with iterators rather than push_back(),
> and it should be faster:
>
>   http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/vector/vector/assign/
>
> Both Eigen::Matrix and std::vector guarantee contiguous memory.
>
> c.  They can both be const, as in:
>
>    virtual void get_params(std::vector<double>& values) const;
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  For future reference:
>
>    For std::vector, thex .at(i) method checks bounds, whereas operator[] doesn't.
>    You shouldn't need to check given that you're looping on size.
>
>    I take it the fact that they all use q.size() is intended?  It's
>    more idiomatic to use the variable you're walking through and should
>    also be easier for a compiler to optimize.

>
>
>
>

messages.subject: Re: bin/print & read_stan_csv input doc + digits
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, June 3, 2013 4:57:02 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Also, would it be possible to get one more digit of printing
> in RStan?  I know Andrew likes minimal, but I almost always want
> at least 2 digits.

The print() function has a digits argument, i.e.

print(fit, digits = 2)

and the print() function is what is ultimately being called when you just type

fit

You can circumvent the Andrew behavior by typing

setMethod("show", "stanfit", def = function(object) print(object, digits = 2))

which will persist for that R session.

Ben

On Tuesday, June 4, 2013 12:25:12 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> ?? I'm lost? What would this be used for?

Here is what it would look like in R code for the standard normal distribution:

# Pick population parameters
# In Stan, these would be var types rather than doubles
# although the the foo_rng() functions only take doubles I think
mu <- 0
sigma <- 1

# Generate large sample from this population
SIMS <- 100000
X <- rnorm(SIMS, mu, sigma)

# Calculate derivatives
# In Stan, this would entail evaluating the gradient of normal_log(X, mu, sigma)
# In R, I just do the gradient analytically
score <- function(x, mu, sigma) c( (x - mu) / sigma^2, (mu^2 - sigma^2 + x^2 - 2 * mu * x) / sigma^3 )
partials <- t(sapply(X, score, mu = mu, sigma = sigma))
colMeans(partials) # small because at the mode

But even better would be to extract the Hessian when normal_log(X, mu, sigma) is evaluated in Stan, get the inverse of the estimated information matrix, and conduct a score test. In R, this is like

I_inv <- diag(c(sigma^2 / SIMS, 2 * sigma^4 / SIMS)) # known analytically
grad <- colSums(partials)
grad %*% I_inv %*% grad # ~ chi-squared with length(grad) degrees of freedom

So, if that test is rejected, then either

-- SIMS was too small
-- there is a rare Type I error
-- the foo_rng function in Stan is wrong
-- the gradient is wrong
-- the Hessian is wrong

But it would be better if this could be automated as much as possible. Definitely drawing the sample, extracting the gradient and Hessian, and conducting the score test is automatable. Setting the population parameters is a bit tricky because different distributions have different numbers of parameters and different restrictions on them.

Ben

We don't need to mix fvar<var> and var.   If there's
an autodiff type, all the autodiff types must be the
same (sort of like vector lengths).

But you do need double.  So just replace the bare
var with double and that's what we want to test for
fvar<var>.

I'd say the place to start is with the derivatives
we're going to need for RM-HMC.  That's all the
things that are in autodiff.hpp.

I should add some doc for that indicating which
instantiations we need for each function concept.

To get all of these operations with double outputs,
we need these:

   autodiff.hpp function     autodiff scalar    order
   -----------------------   ---------------    -----
   gr_tr_mat_times_hessian   fvar<fvar<var>>      3
   hessian                   fvar<var>            2
   hessian_times_vector      fvar<var>            2
   gradient_dot_vector       var                  1
   gradient                  var                  1

   jacobian                  var                  1
                             fvar<double>         1

We don't have any use for the Jacobian planned in
the immediate future.

So that means we need tests for

    fvar<var>
    fvar<fvar<var>>

There is also:

    fvar<double>
    fvar<fvar<double>>

But we don't really foresee any use for these because
fvar<double> only computes a single derivative (dx1) and
fvar<fvar<double>> only a pair of derivatives and a second
derivative (dx1, dx2 and dx1.dx2).

And it's not just distributions, it's all of our functions
that we need to test.

We don't have second or third order finite diffs for testing.

- Bob

messages.subject: stringstream and Scientific Notation
messages.body_plain:
I tracked down the bug in bin/print, and it occurs when string stream tries to parse a number in scientific notation with three digits in the exponent, for example "ss >> 1.78358e-321".  The stream fails, and then further uses of operator>> read from random memory, hence the incorrect results.

Curious.    The number is between min() and denorm_min() for doubles:

   std::cout << "1.78358e-321=" << 1.78358e-321 << std::endl;
   std::cout << "min=" << std::numeric_limits<double>::min() << std::endl;
   std::cout << "denorm min=" << std::numeric_limits<double>::denorm_min() << std::endl;

prints:

   1.78358e-321=1.78358e-321
   min=2.22507e-308
   denorm min=4.94066e-324

My go-to reference

   http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/limits/numeric_limits/

says min() is:

   Minimum finite value.
   For floating types with denormalization (variable number of exponent bits):
   minimum positive normalized value.
   Equivalent to CHAR_MIN, SCHAR_MIN, SHRT_MIN, INT_MIN, LONG_MIN, LLONG_MIN, FLT_MIN,
   DBL_MIN, LDBL_MIN or 0, depending on type.

and for denorm_min(), it  says:

   Minimum positive denormalized value.
   For types not allowing denormalized values: same as min().

I have no idea what denormalization is, but it looks relevant here.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stringstream and Scientific Notation
messages.body_plain:
In IEEE floating point, the number is represented in two parts.  The base number and the exponent, i.e., 1.423566 x 10^-123 (except in base 2) where 1.423566 is the base and -123 is, obviously, the exponent.

There are a certain number of bits given to represent the base and the exponent.  Once the maximum value of the exponent has been reached, that is basically the min value.  However, you can get a slight more range by allowing the base number to be denormalized.  I.E., if you write 0.0000001 x 10^-123, that is a denormalied base.

I would be surprised if this is related to what is going on here.

Cheers,
Marcus

remains consistent between the doc and the code.

however Michael thinks makes most sense.

> I'm writing out examples for the paper to check that it's

> # Diagonal elements of inverse mass matrix:
> # 0.529535
>
> Shouldn't "Step size" now be "time interval" or something
> like that?

Why would it be called that?  We're always discretizing the flow with a numerical integrator by choosing a step size.

> And can we be super-specific and say the following?
>
>  "Diagonal elements of diagonal inverse mass matrix:"

Is metric too esoteric?  I would love to get rid of the "mass matrix" terminology.

In any case, we could have

"Elements of the diagonal (inverse mass matrix/inverse metric)"
"Elements of the (inverse mass matrix/inverse metric)"

> I also thought the header was going to change names for
> things, too:
>
>   lp__,accept_stat__,stepsize__,treedepth__,theta
>
> What is accept_stat__?  I couldn't find a previous discussion
> on the stan-dev list or in the latest manual.

accept_stat is the Metropolis acceptance probability.  I haven't doc'd anything in the manual -- can we start a separate thread/issue noting which items need to be documented?  With all of the changes in place I'm kind of lost as to what should be put into the manual.

> remains consistent between the doc and the code.
>
> Then we can deprecate direct access to lp__ and print the header
> however Michael thinks makes most sense.

Anything descriptive, whether it be "log_prob" or "log_post", of even "log_posterior".

Huh -- when I try to read such a number (albeit in a comma separated list), operator>> flips the fail switch and y gets nonsense.  Killing one of the digits in the exponent removes the problem.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stringstream and Scientific Notation
messages.body_plain:
Yes.  That's really lousy behavior.  No idea what
the full spec is, so I don't know if it's a bug or if
input is undetermined after an error.

With:

   std::stringstream ss;
   double y1, y2;
   std::string punct;
   ss << "2.9e-200, 3.14";
   ss >> y1 >> punct >> y2;
   std::cout << "y1=" << y1 << "; y2=" << y2 << "; punct=" << punct << std::endl;

I get:

   y1=2.9e-200; y2=3.14; punct=,

but with ss set to underflow,

   ss << "2.9e-400, 3.14";

I get:

   y1=0; y2=0; punct=

But then I tried first setting y1 and y2 and
noticed that in the error case you get no change to the variables.
So with

   std::stringstream ss;
   double y1 = 152, y2 = -3;
   std::string punct;
   ss << "2.9e-400, 3.14";
   ss >> y1 >> punct >> y2;
   std::cout << "y1=" << y1 << "; y2=" << y2 << "; punct=" << punct << std::endl;

I got:

   y1=152; y2=-3; punct=

Same results under clang++ and g++ under -O1 and -O3 by the way.

- Bob

On 6/7/13 3:54 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:

> On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 3:51 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com <mailto:goodri...@gmail.com>> wrote:
>
>     On Friday, June 7, 2013 3:29:40 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>         One issue is whether we're going to change lp__, which is
>         used in the models.  I like the idea of adding a function to
>         increment lp__, so I'll make a pull request for that.
>
>
>     Can you make the lp_increment() function take a second "warning" argument that defaults to 1, so that the .stan file
>     can do something like
>
>     if (condition) lp_increment(negative_infinity(), 0);
>
>     in which case, the sampler would immediately reject the proposal without spitting out any long messages and without
>     doing any more calculations for that proposal?
>
>
> Ben, are you sure you don't want a reject() function rather than overloading lp_increment()?

I prefer reject(), or even better, an even more explicit

    raise_exception(...);

Given that we have optimization, etc., "rejection" isn't the
only thing we do.  Then it would make sense to allow these
in the transformed data and generated quantities blocks, which
wouldn't ordinarly be able to "reject" because they don't have
access to lp__.

Conditionals would also slow down the usual lp_increment() behavior,
and if we do what Marcus was suggesting in accumulating a vector to
sum, we should actually be able to speed it up.

- Bob

from write_array is row major or column major.  Now the output

to detect whether it is row / column major order.

Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Argument Refactor
messages.body_plain:
When we discussed this a while ago one idea was to have nuts, bfgs, nesterov, etc be separate commands and then sample and optimize would alias to whatever we wanted the default to be.  This would make some things easier since, for instance, bfgs and nesterov will take a completely different set of parameters.  Or rather, they would if it was possible.  BFGS doesn't have much in the way of user visible options right now, but I would like to change that if it wouldn't pollute the overall options space.

I like the var=val convention as I think it's clearer.

I think it also makes sense to have some global options as well.  E.G., data and init, although maybe it's just best to reimplement them for each subcommand in case we need to do specialization like an init for an ensemble sampler.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Argument Refactor
messages.body_plain:
On 6/8/13 12:07 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> When we discussed this a while ago one idea was to have nuts, bfgs, nesterov, etc be separate commands and then sample
> and optimize would alias to whatever we wanted the default to be.

I think this makes sense.  We can always add a default
"sample" and "optimize" command later.

> This would make some things easier since, for
> instance, bfgs and nesterov will take a completely different set of parameters.

Right.

One implication of this is that the default sampler or optimizer
shouldn't have any options, because they'd change if the
defaults changed.

Thinking about this, I'm wondering if defaults will be more
trouble than they're worth.

> Or rather, they would if it was
> possible.  BFGS doesn't have much in the way of user visible options right now, but I would like to change that if it
> wouldn't pollute the overall options space.
>
> I like the var=val convention as I think it's clearer.

I agree.

> I think it also makes sense to have some global options as well.  E.G., data and init, although maybe it's just best to
> reimplement them for each subcommand in case we need to do specialization like an init for an ensemble sampler.

I think they can share code, at least, if
they have similar functionality.  For doc,
we can have the options be hierarchical, but
each command should just dump out its own complete
doc.

   ./model nuts --help

would dump out help options just for NUTS.  But then I
suppose that could refer to things it inherits from general
HMC, which in turn inherits options from Metropolis,
which inherits methods from MCMC, ...

- Bob

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hmm, this is disturbing.  We should figure out what is going on here.
A

On Jun 9, 2013, at 8:59 AM, Adam Slez wrote:

> Bob, Ben, and Andrew,
>
> I redid the analysis used to produce the previous speed tests which, I forgot to mention, were only based on 2K iterations (hence why some of the R-hats were so high).  Here's what is going on in the setup of the new tests:
>
> 1.  I used 4 chains with 10K iterations.
>
> 2.  I estimated three additional models.  As per Bob's suggestion, the first uses the Matt trick as before, but initial values are set to zero.  The second uses the Matt trick, but the x variable has been mean centered via the use of a transformed data block.  The third model also uses a mean-centered x, but does not use the Matt trick.
>
> 3.  Output was produced using the monitor command so as to ensure comparability between Stan and JAGS, as per the discussion here.  This speaks to Bob's question regarding the calculation of effective sample size.  One thing I noticed is that the monitor results did not match the print results.  I might expect this when looking at the JAGS output, but this also happened in Stan as well.  My understanding is that the print output in Stan is based on the summary function.  How do the summary calculations differ from the monitor calculations?
>
> Here's my reading of the findings:
>
> 1.  JAGS outpaces Stan by quite a bit, regardless of how the model is specified in Stan.
>
> 2.  Stan models which use the Matt trick seem to do worse than Stan models without the Matt trick.
>
> 3.  Models with and without the Matt trick differ in terms of which parameters they are able to efficiently estimate.  Models with the Matt trick do better with respect to bx as compared to u0 or sigma.  The opposite holds for models without the Matt trick.
>
> 4.  Mean centering doesn't seem to help much.
>
> 5.  To speak to Bob's earlier question, in terms of posterior variance Stan actually seems to be doing slightly better when we look at the standard deviation.  Things are obviously a bit different when we look at, say, the standard error of the mean which corrects for effective sample size. Overall, JAGS seems to be doing better here, in large part because of the fact that Stan does well with either u0 and sigma or bx, but not both.  More specifically, we see Stan without the Matt trick doing better than JAGS with to the standard error of the mean for u0 and sigma.  In contrast, if we either center x or set initial values to 0, we see Stan with the Matt trick doing better than JAGS with respect to the standard error of the mean for bx.
>
> I have also attached the diagnostics requested by Bob and Ben.  These include both a traceplot for u0, sigma, and bx, as well as the pairs graph depicting chain-specific results (chains 1 and 2 are on the first page, while chains 3 and 4 are on the second).  To show the correlation between parameter estimates, I have also included a scatterplot matrix depicting draws for u0, sigma, bx, and five randomly chosen group effects (both transformed and untransformed). I'm not sure whether this is the best approach for answering Bob's question as to whether the traceplots show high correlation of the u0, sigma, and e_u variables.  In the first place, I'm not sure that what I did even counts as a traceplot in the usual sense. It would also be preferable to look at all of the u and e_u terms, but I couldn't think of a good way to do this given that I have 144 groups and, hence, 288 + 3 = 291 parameters to graph.  All graphs correspond to the row in the table labeled "Stan w/Matt" (i.e. I used the Matt trick but did not center x or force initial values to 0).
>
> My read is that the chains for u0 and sigma aren't mixing especially well (at least not compared to bx) and that there is some correlation between sigma, u, and e_u, though maybe not a crazy amount.  The u terms seem okay, there is some evidence of correlation between sigma and the e_u terms, and there is definitely correlation among the e_u terms themselves.  Again, this approach is less than perfect because I'm only looking at a handful of u/e_u terms.  Things could be worse elsewhere in the model.
>
> Adam
>
> On Friday, June 7, 2013 11:29:26 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > On Friday, June 7, 2013 10:39:53 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > I'm curious about what's going on here conceptually.
> > >
> > > With the Matt trick, you sample
> > >
> > >    e_u ~ normal(0,1)
> > >
> > > and then set:
> > >
> > >    u <- u0 + sigma * e_u
> > >
> > > u0, sigma, and e_u all have low n_eff (< 70)
> > > whereas u has a high n_eff (2,000).
> > >
> > > Is it the extra variability of the three variables combined
> > > that gives u relatively low autocorrelation?
> >
> > This is odd. I would be interested to see the joint distribution of u0 and sigma, which can be done via rstan with something like
> >
> > pairs(model2, pars = c("u0", "sigma"), chain_id = c(1,2))
> >
> > in this case the results for chain 1 will be in the lower triangle and chain 2 will be in the upper triangle. I would bet at least one of the chains is messed up.
> >
> > Ben
> >

messages.subject: user-defined stuff
messages.body_plain:
The TO-DO file has a number of references to user-defined stuff. As a simple starting point, can we

-- add a grammar rule so that any function in the .stan file whose name ends in __ (or some other magic character combination) is parsed as a literal C++ function call
-- amend the target in the makefile so if a directory contains both foo.stan and foo.hpp, then after parsing foo.stan to foo.cpp the make call is like

$(CC) -include foo.hpp -c -o foo.o foo.cpp

which according to the documentation of g++ and clang++ is equivalent to manually adding

#include "foo.hpp"

at the very top of foo.cpp. That way a user could declare / define a function like bar__() in foo.hpp and use bar__() in foo.cpp that is generated from foo.stan.

That seems easy and unlikely to break any existing code, although users would be on their own when utilizing anything in foo.hpp. It also lowers the barrier where someone maybe wants to try something out before deciding to make the effort to get it included in Stan.

Ben

messages.subject: templated trigamma function
messages.body_plain:
Copyright is for a specific rendering of the algorithm in
code, not for the algorithm itself.

The author of the code you link cites this paper as the
source of the algorithm:

//    BE Schneider,
//    Algorithm AS 121:
//    Trigamma Function,
//    Applied Statistics,
//    Volume 27, Number 1, pages 97-99, 1978.

So I'd suggest just writing a fresh C++ version based on
the journal algorithm above.

There's also a remark, which I haven't read, that might be
worth reading:

   Remark AS R88: A Remark on Algorithm AS 121: The Trigamma Function
   Brian J. Francis
   Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series C (Applied Statistics)
   Vol. 40, No. 3 (1991), pp. 514-515
   (article consists of 2 pages)
   Published by: Wiley for the Royal Statistical Society

And make sure it's templated and differentiable itself so we can do
higher-order derivatives.

At that point, it's probably not going to look like the other
code very much, so we should be OK on copyright.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] user-defined stuff
messages.body_plain:
On June 10, 2013 08:19:49 PM EDT, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Monday, June 10, 2013 7:22:36 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> What namespace should they declare the function in or should they
>> just make it global?  We only having "using" statements for some parts
>> of Stan.
>>
>
> I would think global would usually be fine, but if someone is capable of
> using this plugin mechanism they are probably capable of figuring out what
> needs to go in what namespace.

Stan doesn't (currently) allow "::" in function names, so there'd be
no way to get a user namespace in.  They'd have to define it in one of
the ones we already include.

> Anyway, we just need to make a couple of
> safe changes and then it's their problem if it doesn't work.

I don't quite look at things this way.  We can make safe changes, but
then we need to (a) document them, and (b) help users get them working
when they write to us.  The simpler the mechanism is, the easier these
two tasks are.  Gradually piling on complexity, even if each incremental
change is no big deal, can add up in making a system hard to understand
or debug.

- Bob

Dan,

How about `model help` just prints the valid arguments and prompts the user to call help on the individual argument?  In any case, should the printing of the valid arguments include the verbose information (but without printing any help on child arguments) or just the name of the command?

Any preference on the behavior of the subcommand?  In particular, between:

a)

Calling `model <argument> help` just prints information on the immediate child arguments but stops there.  Users would have to dig through the hierarchy one layer at time to go deeper.

If so, same question as above -- print verbose information or just a list of valid child arguments?

b)

Calling `model <argument> help` prints information about the child arguments and their child arguments recursively.

c)

All arguments have a help and help-all option.  help prints the immediate child arguments, help-all prints all child arguments recursively.

-Mike

messages.body_plain:
On 6/12/13 10:46 AM, Peter Li wrote:
> For to_vector(), what's the return type? vector of vectors?

Just a vector.  The point is to convert a matrix
to a vector.  As in:

    matrix[M,N] a;
    vector[M * N] b;

    b <- to_vector(a);

And it should probably be dumped out column major for
efficiency:

    a[m,n] == b[(n - 1) * M + m]

e.g., for M = 2, N = 3

    b[1] = a[1,1]
    b[2] = a[2,1]
    b[3] = a[1,2]
    b[4] = a[2,2]
    b[5] = a[1,3]
    b[6] = a[2,3]

This should be able to be done without iterating by
grabbing the data of an Eigen matrix, which is an
array in column-major order.  You can then probably
use Eigen::Map to construct the vector to return.

The reason this is nice is that we can use it to vectorize
some operations like univariate densities to matrices without making
the user write out a loop.

This shouldn't be much work, but it's also not a super high
priority.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
While waiting for acid_tests to run I spent some time looking through the ensemble literature, eventually going back to the original Goodman and Weare paper on which emcee is based.  Unlike the emcee paper (on the arXiv, glosses over waaaaaay too many details) Goodman and Weare treat the ensemble sampler as a Markov chain on the product space pi cross pi .... pi cross pi, and explicitly note that any the sequence of any particular walker is very much NOT a Markov chain.  In the end, though, they get tricky.  When comparing ESS between a single chain and the ensemble, they collapse the ensemble at each sample by averaging each walker to produce f_{i} = sum_{j} f (x_{ij}), where i indexes time and j the walkers.  They then compare ESS/accuracy using both 1D chains.

messages.body_plain:
On 6/13/13 12:54 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> While waiting for acid_tests to run I spent some time looking through the ensemble literature, eventually going back to
> the original Goodman and Weare paper on which emcee is based.  Unlike the emcee paper (on the arXiv, glosses over
> waaaaaay too many details) Goodman and Weare treat the ensemble sampler as a Markov chain on the product space pi cross
> pi .... pi cross pi, and explicitly note that any the sequence of any particular walker is very much NOT a Markov chain.

Right. Their equation (5) states (but does not explain why)
that for J walkers at iteration i, you have:

  p(x_{i,1},...,x{i,J}) = p(x_{i,1}) ... p(x_{i,J})

I'd like to understand why.  It seems wrong to me given
that x_{i,j} depends on x_{i-1,j} and also at least two
other points, other x_{i-1,j'} and x_{i-1,j''}.

>   In the end, though, they get tricky.  When comparing ESS between a single chain and the ensemble, they collapse the
> ensemble at each sample by averaging each walker to produce f_{i} = sum_{j} f (x_{ij}), where i indexes time and j the
> walkers.  They then compare ESS/accuracy using both 1D chains.

In section 3, they seem to be restricting attention to estimating
posterior expectations means.

> So one possibility for Stan is to output not output the full product space in samples.csv (or have multiple output
> files, one for each walker) and then have bin/print produce any summary stats using the above method.  Any nonlinear
> expectations needed by the user can be accommodated by adding transformed parameters in the original model.
> Thoughts?

We want to do full Bayesian inference, so just averaging over
walkers j isn't going to help us because the posterior
variance will be too low.  But, if that can compute a reasonable
effective sample size that we could use with all the samples,
that could work.

But if each walker itself isn't a Markov chain, then we can't
even just use one chain.  So I'm not sure what we can do with
the "samples."

- Bob

> Right. Their equation (5) states (but does not explain why)
> that for J walkers at iteration i, you have:
>
>  p(x_{i,1},...,x{i,J}) = p(x_{i,1}) ... p(x_{i,J})
>
> I'd like to understand why.  It seems wrong to me given
> that x_{i,j} depends on x_{i-1,j} and also at least two
> other points, other x_{i-1,j'} and x_{i-1,j''}.

Yup, each point in the ensemble depends on each other -- that's why the individual sequences are not Markov chains.  But if you treat the ensemble as a state, {x_{0, j}, …, x_{i, j}, … x_{I, j}} then the distribution of the ensemble is preserved by each move.  Basically you're parameters are the parameters of the full state and you're just Gibbs sampling when you update one of the walkers.

> In section 3, they seem to be restricting attention to estimating
> posterior expectations means.

Which, to be fair, is about all you can do with MCMC samples.

> We want to do full Bayesian inference, so just averaging over
> walkers j isn't going to help us because the posterior
> variance will be too low.  But, if that can compute a reasonable
> effective sample size that we could use with all the samples,
> that could work.

But you don't use the posterior variance of that average.  You average x_{j} = 1 / I \sum_{i} x_{ij}, and the sequence { x_{j} } becomes a valid Markov chain.  You compute your expectations, variances, ESS, and MCSE from those averages.  In fact it's actually more conservative than treating each chain as independent and weighting the samples by the individual chain ESSs.

> But if each walker itself isn't a Markov chain, then we can't
> even just use one chain.  So I'm not sure what we can do with
> the "samples."

If you just took one walker and threw everything else out, then you'd have a Markov chain.  If you repeated the same process with each walker you'd have something that looked like a Markov chain but together they'd be correlated and so you couldn't treat them independently.  By averaging you get around the correlations, but become sensitive to chains that haven't converged (I think you can get around this by using the median).

Basically, you can't use each individual walker as a separate draw.  But if you map ( x_{0, j}, …, x_{i, j}, … x_{I, j} )  -> x_{j}, say via an average or a median, for a given time index j then you get a sequence of draws that is a proper Markov chain.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
> Why is the average of the J walkers a Markov chain?  If
> mu[i] is the average at i, I can't see how to formulate
>
>  p(mu[i] | mu[i-1])
>
> Is there something general that says a transform of a Markov
> chain is a Markov chain?  If so, that'd explain why both the
> average and the projection to one walker form Markov chains.

Just consider the multivariate case: you have a Markov chain sampling from some p(x1, x2).  You can transform to p( x2 ) = int dx1 p(x1, x2) at each state, so that { x2 } are valid draws from a Markov chain for p( x2 ).

The proof is straightforward.  Let T be a Markov transition with invariant density pi(x1, x2).  Then by definition

pi(x1, x2) = int dx1' dx2' T (x1, x2 | x1', x2' ) pi(x1', x2').

Integrating both sides with respect to x2 gives

int dx2 pi(x1, x2) = int dx2 dx1' dx2' T (x1, x2 | x1', x2' ) pi(x1', x2')

or

pi(x1) = int dx1' [ int dx2 dx2' T(x1, x2 | x1', x2') pi(x1', x2') / pi(x1') ] pi(x1')

pi(x1) = int dx1' [ int dx2 dx2' T(x1, x2 | x1', x2') pi(x2' | x1') ] pi(x1')

Where

T(x1 | x1') \equiv int dx2 dx2' T(x1, x2 | x1', x2') pi(x2' | x1')

is a valid Markov transition for pi(x1).

Neal talks about the general case in his ensemble paper, and the intuition is really nice.  The marginalized transition first samples x2 from the condition distribution p(x2 | x1) and then performs a transition on the space (x1, x2) before marginalizing back to just x1.  It's also how HMC works, where x2 is the momenta, x1 the position, and T(x1, x2 | x1', x2') the Hamiltonian flow + Metropolis correction.

You can readily generalize the proof to include changes of variables x1, x2 -> f(x1, x2) (where f(x1, x2) might be the average or the median), and the same reasoning holds for the ensemble where you consider the state space x = {x1, …, xi, … xI}.

> I don't see how you can estimate posterior variance from
> the mu[i], though.  It seems to me that the variance of
> the chain of mu[i] will be lower than that of the component
> walkers.

Right, but you only use the mu[i] to compute the expectation of mu.  If you want the variance then you have to compute var[i, j] in each walker and average that.  While this method does account for the correlations in a systematic way it is terribly inflexible.

> P.S.  Thanks for trying to explain this all to me.

No worries at all.  If people didn't push me to explain I'd get in the habit of handwaving instead of whipping up little proofs like that and understanding it better myself.  Keep me on my toes!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
>> I don't see how you can estimate posterior variance from
>> the mu[i], though.  It seems to me that the variance of
>> the chain of mu[i] will be lower than that of the component
>> walkers.
>
> Right, but you only use the mu[i] to compute the expectation of mu.  If you want the variance then you have to compute var[i, j] in each walker and average that.  While this method does account for the correlations in a systematic way it is terribly inflexible.

Actually, this is exactly the behavior we want!  The variance of the means will indeed shrink, which means the MCSE will also shrink.  But that is the desired behavior -- if the walkers are independent then the MCSE will decrease by 1 / n_walkers, giving MCSE = var / (ESS * n_walkers).  The full power of the samples is preserved.

Yeah, it would be an important for any implementation.

> It also made me realize that the n_eff we report
> is the n_eff for the mean, so that won't carry over to estimating
> variance, either.

Nope, for that you'd need fourth order statistics which no one ever quotes.  I've never seen more than MCSE quoted or used.

> Could we just use the ensemble averages to compute n_eff, then
>
> just go ahead and use all the samples for inference?  Each of the samples
> has the right marginal distribution.  We won't necessarily
> know the n_eff, but then we don't know that for what we have anyway
> unless we compute it on the outside.

You could, but then why did we calculate n_eff?  Correlations don't effect the mean, just the variance/MCSE so users could use ensemble samples or ensemble averages to compute whatever expectation they desire, they'd just have no good idea of its precision.  If we're trying to push users into more "responsible" use of MCMC then we'd have to force them into using that they specified and was averaged, if it's not defined in your model or in the transformed parameters block then we can't make any claim of confidence and so won't let you use it.  At least not use it easily.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
I see n_eff as having three roles:
1.  We use n_eff in our (informal) stopping rules, for example we require n_eff > 10 for all quantities of interest.
2.  n_eff is used in computing the Monte Carlo standard errors
3.  We use n_eff in our efficiency comparisons (seconds of wall time per n_eff).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
On 6/14/13 10:21 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:> I see n_eff as having three roles:

 > 1.  We use n_eff in our (informal) stopping rules, for example we require n_eff > 10 for all quantities of interest.
 > 2.  n_eff is used in computing the Monte Carlo standard errors
 > 3.  We use n_eff in our efficiency comparisons (seconds of wall time per n_eff).

 > On Jun 14, 2013, at 5:15 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
 >>
 >> You could, but then why did we calculate n_eff?  Correlations
 >> don't effect the mean, just the variance/MCSE so users could use ensemble samples or ensemble averages to compute
 >> whatever expectation they desire, they'd just have no good idea of its precision.

 >> If we're trying to push users
 >> into more "responsible" use of MCMC then we'd have to force them into using that they specified and was averaged, if
 >> it's not defined in your model or in the transformed parameters block then we can't make any claim of confidence and
 >> so won't let you use it.  At least not use it easily.

This is exactly what I'm worried about.  And not
just for ensemble methods.

We report posterior sd and posterior quantiles, but
we only report n_eff for the mean.  What's our
certainty on the posterior quantile and sd estimates?

We can calculate theta^2 in a single sample, but not
variance or sd or quantiles, because they depend on
multiple samples.   In comparing systems, Matt had
been using theta^2 for all variables theta of interest
to get a handle on how well posterior variance was being
estimated.

Other expectations, like event probabilities, can be pretty
easily calculated by defining variables using indicator
functions.  These should have their uncertainties calculated
properly.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
> > 1.  We use n_eff in our (informal) stopping rules, for example we require n_eff > 10 for all quantities of interest.
> > 2.  n_eff is used in computing the Monte Carlo standard errors
> > 3.  We use n_eff in our efficiency comparisons (seconds of wall time per n_eff).

Agreed.  The only issue is that all three require knowing the expectation of interest a priori.

> This is exactly what I'm worried about.  And not
> just for ensemble methods.
>
> We report posterior sd and posterior quantiles, but
> we only report n_eff for the mean.  What's our
> certainty on the posterior quantile and sd estimates?

I'm not sure about the quantiles, but you can compute the variance of the variance and define a MCSE the same as for the mean.  In practice, however, the uncertainty o the variance isn't as critical -- it's the uncertainty of the posterior uncertainty and second-order in some sense.

> We can calculate theta^2 in a single sample, but not
> variance or sd or quantiles, because they depend on
> multiple samples.   In comparing systems, Matt had
> been using theta^2 for all variables theta of interest
> to get a handle on how well posterior variance was being
> estimated.

Right -- technically the variance is a function of the data and an unknown constant (the mean).  It can be calculated via the expectations of theta and theta^{2}, however, which would be straightforward to implement in both the single state and ensemble schemes.

> Other expectations, like event probabilities, can be pretty
> easily calculated by defining variables using indicator
> functions.  These should have their uncertainties calculated
> properly.

Here's the way I see the grand scheme of things.  One of the great features of MCMC is that the samples can be transformed or marginalized trivially, without changing their validity.  That means you can run your sampler and still have valid inference even if you decide that you're interested in different expectations.  On the other hand, this flexibility requires the user to compute ESS themselves.  We can handle the calculations automatically, provided the user define the desired expectations a priori.  This leave three approaches

One Stage Stan:

All expectations have to be defined in the model or transformed parameters.  We run the model, compute mean, variance, ESS, and MCSE automatically and report those summary statistics.

One Point Five Stage Stan:

We compute the summary statistics automatically as above, but store the intermediate samples in case an expert user wants to change the expectations.

Two Stage Stan:

Sampling and post-processing are two completely different stages, and we rewrite bin/print to be less reliant on the Stan format and assume little more than a csv.

Currently, Stan uses the middle strategy.  One Stage Stan would be more user friendly but slightly more annoying for expert users.  Of course, it wouldn't be hard to make the approach customizable.

On Saturday, June 15, 2013 11:00:38 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> This is exactly what I'm worried about.  And not
> just for ensemble methods.
>
> We report posterior sd and posterior quantiles, but
> we only report n_eff for the mean.  What's our
> certainty on the posterior quantile and sd estimates?

And the n_eff is only applicable to the marginal mean. Perhaps that is okay if the user were only interested in some treatment effect. But it really doesn't make sense for the multivariate parameters such as the simplex, correlation matrix, etc. where a user pretty much can't be interested in the marginal means in isolation. It would be nice if we had some measure of effective sample size for a multivariate parameter as a whole, but in the absence of that, I guess we should be telling users to calculate all quantities of interest in the generated quantities block.

Ben

We could.  Right now, Michael's working on the new commands,
so that'd be the natural place to put it.  Marcus has also
requested more control over inits in the past.

In the past, you (Andrew) said to just use the BUGS inits.
In many cases, these are themselves 0.

with a degree of randomization around them.

> I hope that our new multi-stage adaptation will solve this problem,

That'd be nice. :-)

> P.S.  If we're ever recoding a Bugs model and it runs slow and there
> are any easy fixes (e.g., the Matt trick), we should just put the fix
> in.  We might as well make Stan look as fast as possible.

Anything we do with these globally is a pain because there
are dozens and dozens of them.

It's also not clear the "Matt trick" is always a win.  So
it's going to take some work to find the optimal way to fit
these models in Stan.  That all seems a bit unfair for comparison
unless we do the same for BUGS/JAGS implementations.

We had decided a meeting or two ago that we'd try to build

both a direct translation and a more idiomatic Stan version.
That would allow both the direct comparison, whatever that means, and also
a comparison with a more optimized Stan implementations.

Right now, the models are all over the place in terms of
how much vectorization and other efficiency coding.
If we try to conform to the plan of a baseline and a fast
version, it's going to be a lot of work, because there are
dozens and dozens of models, none of which have very extensive
doc either on the Stan or BUGS side.

Right now, I'm just trying to get them all working and
getting the same answers.

We wanted to compare to JAGS.  To do that with our diffuse
inits, we'd need to take those diffuse inits, constrain them,
then feed them into JAGS.  Right now, most of the BUGS models
get hard-coded inits.  In my experience, many models won't
fit in either Stan or BUGS without reasonable inits.

We also haven't decided what to do about their priors.
The BUGS examples are full of really fat priors, like normal(0,1000)

for parameters with values in single digits.

- Bob

I'm happy to use the Bugs inits when doing head-to-head comparisons, but (a) you said that in some models they don't fully specify the inits, and (b) I don't want 0.000 as a general option; it just seems to me that this could cause trouble.

> with a degree of randomization around them.

Yes, I agree that users should be able to specify inits.  But we do need defaults.

>

> > in.  We might as well make Stan look as fast as possible.

> are dozens and dozens of them.

I'm not saying we should do these globally.  All I'm saying is, if we have a _particular_ model that is running relatively slowly in Stan, _and_ we happen to see an _easy_ way to make it faster, we can just do it.

>
> It's also not clear the "Matt trick" is always a win.  So
> it's going to take some work to find the optimal way to fit
> these models in Stan.

I'm not talking about optimal, I'm just saying that we should feel free to spiff up slow models if that's easy to do.

>  That all seems a bit unfair for comparison
> unless we do the same for BUGS/JAGS implementations.

> version, it's going to be a lot of work, because there are
> dozens and dozens of models, none of which have very extensive
> doc either on the Stan or BUGS side.

I am not saying we should optimize all the models; I'm just saying that, when we're doing the implementations, we can feel free to make them faster if it's not too difficult.

> getting the same answers.

I agree, that's the #1 issue.  Then when we have the scatterplot showing the speed comparisons, if there are any dots on the plot that make Stan look bad, I think it would be ok to take a quick look and see if some vectorization or reparameterization will make it go faster.

>
> We wanted to compare to JAGS.  To do that with our diffuse
> inits, we'd need to take those diffuse inits, constrain them,
> then feed them into JAGS.  Right now, most of the BUGS models
> get hard-coded inits.  In my experience, many models won't
> fit in either Stan or BUGS without reasonable inits.

>
> for parameters with values in single digits.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
On Jun 15, 2013, at 11:00 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> We report posterior sd and posterior quantiles, but
> we only report n_eff for the mean.  What's our
> certainty on the posterior quantile and sd estimates?

I don't see the need, in most cases, to give uncertainties on posterior quantiles and sd's.  If these are desired, we can do so (most simply by computing them separately for each of the split chains and then getting uncertainties that way, more generally by some sort of fft-like approach).  But most of the time I think the important things are the parameters themselves, not the quantiles etc.

messages.body_plain:
We've already discussed that any model that has finite mass at a boundary would not be appropriate for HMC, the easiest way of thinking about it being that after we transform variables such model would have finite mass at +/- infinity, which we certainly can't handle on a computer.  So trying to sample randomly between bounds is a bad idea -- we want to sample uniformly from the typical set, not the entire support.

It looks like -2, 2 is indeed too big for the uninitialized BUGS models, so smaller is probably better.  We can always try small values, [-1, 1] or [-1/2, 1/2], see how the ensemble of models performs.

On Sunday, June 16, 2013 6:49:34 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> We've already discussed that any model that has finite mass at a boundary would not be appropriate for HMC, the easiest way of thinking about it being that after we transform variables such model would have finite mass at +/- infinity, which we certainly can't handle on a computer.

I agree with that, but that seems like problem that is broader than just choosing starting values.

> So trying to sample randomly between bounds is a bad idea -- we want to sample uniformly from the typical set, not the entire support.

You could draw uniformally on half the width of the support if you like that better, but the best thing would be to make it easy for the user to specify (some subset of) initial values, possibly random draws from the prior, in an init block of the .stan file.

> It looks like -2, 2 is indeed too big for the uninitialized BUGS models, so smaller is probably better.  We can always try small values, [-1, 1] or [-1/2, 1/2], see how the ensemble of models performs.

Uniform on (-a,a) with a chosen by the user is better than hard-coding a = 2, but there are so many different transformations that it is hard to set a width on the unbounded scale and have that be good for each bounded parameter. But it would be a step in the right direction. Right now, we have too many situations where we have to start with init=0 just to avoid the initial (-2,2) behavior that ruins the convergence.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] PyStan
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

re: pystan

I'm trying to mirror the api I find in the rstan-dev github repo right now. Are
there significant changes to the RStan api in the works?

My strategy is to have something api compatible with RStan with the following
deviations:

- obvious pythonic replacements: fit.extract(...) instead of extract(fit, ...)
- less obvious pythonic replacements; dictionaries (OrderedDict) instead of
  R lists, numpy arrays instead of R matrices.
- No attempt to allow variables to be referenced by string (e.g. specifying
  model_code or data with a string naming a variable). Python is
  pass-by-reference so there's no need..

I've still got to figure out the install-time compilation of libstan.a and
libstanc.a and the run-time compilation of models. The hard work (wrapping cpp
with Cython) is finished.

I should have something tomorrow, I think. I'll post a link to the github repo.

Best,

Allen

p.s. I'm targeting Python 3.3, Cython 19.1. I don't think backporting to Python
2.7 should be too difficult.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] PyStan
messages.body_plain:
>> - obvious pythonic replacements: fit.extract(...) instead of
>> extract(fit, ...)
>> - less obvious pythonic replacements; dictionaries (OrderedDict) instead of
>>   R lists, numpy arrays instead of R matrices.

Makes sense.  I think ordered dictionaries should be
just like lists if they nest.

>> - No attempt to allow variables to be referenced by string (e.g. specifying
>>   model_code or data with a string naming a variable). Python is
>>   pass-by-reference so there's no need..

We need something like name=value so we know which values
correspond to which variables.  Having the strings just avoided
the R idiom of list(a=a,b=b,...), where the LHS a is a variable
name and the RHS is the value.  But just having c(a,b,c), the
array of values, wouldn't be enough because you wouldn't know what the values
referred to.

- Bob

way possible.  I need to put that into a pull request --- I only
have one univariate function implemented this way.  With the
trick Marcus introduced recently, it should be possible to at least
cut down on the number of virtual function calls, which are relatively
expensive compared to functions doing simple arithmetic.

>
> I just closed the issue.
>
> I was never suggesting to get rid of error checking!  I just
> suspected an issue with the check_not_nan() implementation.
>
> I'll be more careful to measure functions
> independently before submitting another issue based on
> profiling an involved function.  No idea why the profiler showed
> so much time in is_nan().
>
> I couldn't measure a difference (meaning that the between-run
> differences were larger than the code differences) between:
>
>   1. stan::math::check_not_nan<double,double>("fun",x,"x");
>
>   2.  if (x != x) return std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
>
> The timing is also the same with x = NaN and x = 0.01.
>
> I also couldn't measure a difference between clang++ and g++.
>
> Then I thought it might all be branch prediction and then checked
> every other iteration adding NaN and 0.01, which defeats branch
> prediction.  That did have an effect.  It's about 5% slower under
> g++ and 10% slower under clang++.  (So in this case, there was
> a difference between clang++ and g++.)
>
> I'll append the test code.
>
> - Bob
>
> -------------------
> #include <stan/math/error_handling/check_not_nan.hpp>
> #include <iostream>
> #include <limits>
>
> inline double fun(double x) {
>   if (x != x) return std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
>   // stan::math::check_not_nan<double,double>("fun",x,"x");
>   return x;
> }
>
> int main() {
>   double outer_sum = 0;
>   for (int m = 0; m < 10000; ++m) {
>     double sum = 0;
>     for (int n = 0; n < 1000000; ++n)
>       sum += fun(std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN());
>       // sum += fun(0.001);
>       // sum += fun(n % 2 == 0 ? 0.01 : std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN());
>     outer_sum += sum;
>   }
>   std::cout << "outer_sum=" << outer_sum << std::endl;
> }

messages.subject: (G)LM distribution functions
messages.body_plain:
[changed subject, moved to stan-dev]

On 6/21/13 1:08 PM, Peter Li wrote:
>>     I also think we could productively add regression distributions, e.g.
>>
>>        real logistic_regression_log(int y, vector beta, vector x)
>>        =def=
>>        bernoulli_log(y, inv_logit(x' * beta))
>>
>>        real linear_regression_log(real y, vector beta, vector x, real sigma)
>>        =def=
>>        normal_log(y,x' * beta,sigma)
>>
>>
> So for these, do we want to directly return bernoulli_log(y,inv_logit(x' * beta)) and normal_log(y,x'*beta,sigma)?

The motiviation is to make the implementation more efficient.
So you need a new vari type (for reverse mode) and to calculate
the derivatives w.r.t. y, x', beta (and sigma in the
case of linear regression).

I also changed the type of y in the linear case to real.  Now the issue
is that these should be vectorized so that y can be a vector in both
cases.  But we haven't really worked out multivariate vectorizations,
so there's some work to do there on figuring out which signatures to use
and how to implement it.  A very likely way for linear regression to be
called would be as this:

   double linear_regression_log(const Eigen::Vector<double,Dynamic,1>& y,
                                const Eigen::Vector<var,Dynamic,1>& beta,
                                const Eigen::Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>& x)
   =def=

   var sum = 0;
   for (n in 1:size(y))
      sum += normal_log(y[n],x[n] * beta,sigma)

If y is size N and beta is size K, then x is an (N x K) matrix
and x[n] is a K-vector.

But we'd want it to handle all of the double/var alternations as well
as forward mode fvar.

Other generalized linear models could be done the same way,
like
       real poisson_regression_log(int y, vector beta, vector x)
       =def=
       poisson_log_log(y,x' * beta)
       =def=
       poisson_log(y, exp(x' * beta))

The ' is just transpose, but the implementation should be like dot product
so that x and beta can be any vector or array types, and y could also be
vectorized.

- Bob

The issue isn't the -k flag. When you add the parallelization flag with it being greater or equal to 3, make doesn't detect failures properly. The solution is to run it without the -j flag or set it to 2. The other solution is to run the target again after running it once without the -j flag. That will pick up the failure and it won't spend the time compiling.

I believe the way the target is set up, it will compile everything first, so it won't detect failures until runtime if it compiles. You could run a single test if you know what distribution you are testing.

Daniel

On 6/24/13 11:04 AM, Peter Li wrote:
> I don't think I understand what you're saying completely. So for the new vari type, is it supposed to just take in the
> jacobian matrix and compute the determinant?

However you have to implement it, there should be a single
vari for the log Jacobian determinant that gets added to the
log probability parameter being passed in.

The point is to make the entire transform stage of Stan faster.

For example, suppose we have:

parameters {
    real<lower=L> x[N];
    ...
}

The transform to constrained space is

    x[n] |--> exp(x[n]) + L

So the Jacobian is diagonal so the log determinant is
just sum(x).  So you won't even need a new type in
this case.

The lower-bound L may be a variable, but even if it is,
dL/dx = 0 because the bound L can't depend on x because
of variable declaration ordering constraints in Stan (can't
use a variable before it's fully declared).

So why don't you start with this case.

The full set of transforms we use and their Jacobian determinants
are defined in the manual.

> Also, should I separate the transforms into their own files (i.e. refactor like we did for agrad/fvar/math)?

That would be great.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] vectorizing transforms
messages.body_plain:
Now I see the issue.

The model:

   parameters {
     real<lower=0> y[10];
   }
   model {
     y ~ normal(0,1);
   }

translates the constraints to:

         vector<T__> y;
         size_t dim_y_0__ = 10;
         y.reserve(dim_y_0__);
         for (size_t k_0__ = 0; k_0__ < dim_y_0__; ++k_0__) {
             y.push_back(in__.scalar_lb_constrain(0,lp__));
         }

So in order to do what I want, we need to change the generated
code to something like:

    vector<T__> y = in__.scalar_lb_constrain_array(dim_y_0__,0,lp__);

Then scalar_lb_constrain_array() would generate a single vari
instance to add to lp__ for the Jacobian.

So either you're going to have to dive into the generator code
in stan/gm, or wait until I get to it.

- Bob

On 6/24/13 1:18 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> I understand how the jacobian plays into this, but I'm still confused about defining a vari for it and how to use it.
> Right now, I have something like
>
>      template <typename T, typename TL>
>      inline
>      typename return_type<T,TL>::type>::type
>      lb_constrain(const T& x, const TL& lb, T& lp) {
>
>        if (!(stan::length(x)))
>          return 0.0;
>
>        double res(0.0);
>
>        agrad::OperandsAndPartials<T> operands_and_partials(x);
>        VectorView<const T> x_vec(x);
>        size_t N = max_size(x);
>        for (size_t n = 0; n < N; n++) {
>          const double x_dbl = value_of(x_vec[n]);
>
>          lp += x_dbl;
>
>          res += exp(x_dbl) + lb;
>
>          if (!is_constant_struct<T>::value)
>            operands_and_partials.d_x1[n] += exp(x_dbl);
>        }
>
>        return operands_and_partials.to_var(res);
>      }
>
> But I'm not sure how I should be treating res--should it be a vector at least type T to match x?
>
>
> Peter
>
> On 6/24/13 12:07 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>>
>> On 6/24/13 11:04 AM, Peter Li wrote:
>>> I don't think I understand what you're saying completely. So for the new vari type, is it supposed to just take in the
>>> jacobian matrix and compute the determinant?
>>
>> However you have to implement it, there should be a single
>> vari for the log Jacobian determinant that gets added to the
>> log probability parameter being passed in.
>>
>> The point is to make the entire transform stage of Stan faster.
>>
>> For example, suppose we have:
>>
>> parameters {
>>    real<lower=L> x[N];
>>    ...
>> }
>>
>> The transform to constrained space is
>>
>>    x[n] |--> exp(x[n]) + L
>>
>> So the Jacobian is diagonal so the log determinant is
>> just sum(x).  So you won't even need a new type in
>> this case.
>>
>> The lower-bound L may be a variable, but even if it is,
>> dL/dx = 0 because the bound L can't depend on x because
>> of variable declaration ordering constraints in Stan (can't
>> use a variable before it's fully declared).
>>
>> So why don't you start with this case.
>>
>> The full set of transforms we use and their Jacobian determinants
>> are defined in the manual.
>>
>>> Also, should I separate the transforms into their own files (i.e. refactor like we did for agrad/fvar/math)?
>>
>> That would be great.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>

messages.body_plain:
I'm finding a couple things in the output of bin/print confusing.
Here's an example:

------------------------------------------
~/stan(feature/stan-language-paper)$ bin/print --precision=2 samples*.csv
Inference for Stan model: bernoulli_model
4 chains: each with iter=(1000,1000,1000,1000); warmup=(0,0,0,0); thin=(1,1,1,1); 4000 iterations saved.

Warmup took (0.092863, 0.09911, 0.10535, 0.095827) seconds, 0.39315 seconds total
Sampling took (0.089032, 0.088401, 0.097865, 0.087141) seconds, 0.362439 seconds total

                     mean se_mean   sd      2.5%       25%       50%       75%     97.5%    n_eff n_eff/time     Rhat
lp__           -7.30e+00    0.02 0.77 -9.45e+00 -7.49e+00 -7.02e+00 -6.80e+00 -6.75e+00 9.76e+02   2.69e+03 1.00e+00
accept_stat__   5.01e-01    0.05 0.40  2.22e-07  7.52e-02  4.75e-01  9.99e-01  1.00e+00 5.50e+01   1.52e+02 1.03e+00
stepsize__      2.15e+00    0.13 0.19  1.97e+00  1.97e+00  2.14e+00  2.46e+00  2.46e+00 2.00e+00   5.52e+00 5.69e+13
treedepth__     4.60e-02    0.00 0.21  0.00e+00  0.00e+00  0.00e+00  0.00e+00  1.00e+00 2.97e+03   8.19e+03 1.00e+00
theta           2.53e-01    0.00 0.12  5.94e-02  1.59e-01  2.35e-01  3.32e-01  5.42e-01 1.76e+03   4.84e+03 1.00e+00

Samples were drawn using NUTS with a diagonal Euclidean metric.
For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
convergence, Rhat=1).
------------------------------------------------

I like the warmup and sampling times and the more
explicit indication of the chains.  I also like that it's
now dumping the accept stat, stepsize and tree depth.

What is the accept stat?

I still find "thin" a confusing name. I think "keep" is more in line
with the behavior, because thin=1 keeps every sample.  If thin=2,
you keep every other sample, and if thin=3, you keep every third sample.

I believe the warmup=(0,0,0,0) indicates that the samples.csv didn't have
warmup "samples"?  I'm worried people are going to run Stan then find
this confusing if our default isn't to save and mark warmup "samples".

Shouldn't "precision=2" lead to 2 digits rather than 3 digits of precision?

Is the stepsize sd just because there are four chains?

Can we change n_eff/time to n_eff/s?  That does seem to be the unit.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: CDF values > 1
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for reporting.   I'm cc-ing stan-dev.

Can we change the behavior of the CDFs to
do this internally without changing their derivatives?
That way we can have the best of both worlds.

The problem with the proposed solution

 >      otherResponseCDF <- if_else(otherResponseCDF>1,1,otherResponseCDF);

is that when the condition is true, you lose the connection
to the derivative.  This may not be apparent in a large model,
but it's not the right thing to do.

- Bob

On 6/25/13 7:55 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> After a lot of playing around, it seems that the culprit is indeed the fact that "otherResponseCDF" is occasionally
> greater than 1, causing log1m() to throw an error. Actually, it's only ever minutely greater than 1 (ex. 1+1.04361e-14,
> 1+6.21725e-15, etc), so I suspect this is a precision issue of some sort (I'm only vaguely familiar with the idea that
> computers can have trouble representing numbers precisely) . Adding the line:
>
>      otherResponseCDF <- if_else(otherResponseCDF>1,1,otherResponseCDF);
>
> solves things.
>
>
>
> On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 4:44:32 PM UTC-3, Mike Lawrence wrote:
>
>     Thanks for the help (and apologies for failing to add a subject line!).
>
>     I must be failing to properly constrain the range of one of the variables somewhere. I have to head out for a bit
>     now, but I'll play some more this evening and report back to resolve the thread.
>
>
>
>     On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 3:33:23 PM UTC-3, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
>         On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 1:57:44 PM UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
>
>             Any suggestions as to what I should do next to track down what's going awry?
>
>
>         It's the last line
>
>         |
>
>         |
>         lp__ <- lp__ + (log1m(otherResponseCDF)+log(thisResponsePDF));
>         |
>
>         |
>         log1m() requires its argument to be <= 1, which isn't guaranteed to be the case in your model. Actually, I think
>         it is guaranteed to not be the case as written:
>
>         |
>
>         otherResponseCDF <- 1+(tmp1+tmp2)/thisStartMax[subject[i]];
>
>         |
>
>         If tmp1, tmp2, and thisStartMax[subject[i]] are all positive then otherResponseCDF is always going to greater
>         than 1.
>
>         Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format for bin/print?
messages.body_plain:
> What is the accept stat?

Metropolis acceptance probability.

> I still find "thin" a confusing name. I think "keep" is more in line
> with the behavior, because thin=1 keeps every sample.  If thin=2,
> you keep every other sample, and if thin=3, you keep every third sample.

Thin is the notation used in BDA -- it's an easy fix on the Stan side is we decide to change it.  I have no strong opinions.

> I believe the warmup=(0,0,0,0) indicates that the samples.csv didn't have
> warmup "samples"?  I'm worried people are going to run Stan then find
> this confusing if our default isn't to save and mark warmup "samples".

Right, the numbers refer to what was saved.  We can add a note making it more explicit, but I think it's safer to default to not saving, as otherwise people might use the warmup samples as regular samples and really mess up their inferences.

> The timing should be printed with the same precision as everything else.

I can fix that.  Can you create an issue with the various changes you'd like and assign me?

> Shouldn't "precision=2" lead to 2 digits rather than 3 digits of precision?

Well, yes, but there is a subtly.  Here you have numbers like 0.12 -- since there's nothing to the left of the decimal you have two digits of precision to the right.  But if everything in the column is shown with the same width, then other numbers will have to go from 4.2 to 4.21.

> Is the stepsize sd just because there are four chains?

Yup.

> Can we change n_eff/time to n_eff/s?  That does seem to be the unit.

Sure.  I originally wanted "neff/time (samples/s)" but that was way too verbose.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format for bin/print?
messages.body_plain:
On 6/26/13 3:33 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> What is the accept stat?
>
> Metropolis acceptance probability.

For what?  NUTS doesn't just generate a proposal then Metropolis
accept/reject.

>> I still find "thin" a confusing name. I think "keep" is more in line
>> with the behavior, because thin=1 keeps every sample.  If thin=2,
>> you keep every other sample, and if thin=3, you keep every third sample.
>
> Thin is the notation used in BDA -- it's an easy fix on the Stan side is we decide to change it.  I have no strong opinions.

I know.  It's also used in the other packages.

I just thought that this would be the time to change it.
In the same spirit as changing "burnin" to "warmup",
we could change "thin" to "keep" or something similar.

>> I believe the warmup=(0,0,0,0) indicates that the samples.csv didn't have
>> warmup "samples"?  I'm worried people are going to run Stan then find
>> this confusing if our default isn't to save and mark warmup "samples".
>
> Right, the numbers refer to what was saved.  We can add a note making it more explicit, but I think it's safer to default to not saving, as otherwise people might use the warmup samples as regular samples and really mess up their inferences.

I think that makes sense from the command-line.  It's a little
different in R because of the way things like traceplots are generated
and how the accessors are implemented to let you ignore the
warmup iterations.

>> The timing should be printed with the same precision as everything else.
>
> I can fix that.  Can you create an issue with the various changes you'd like and assign me?

That's the only definite one at the moment.

There's also the issue of printing every iteration.

>> Shouldn't "precision=2" lead to 2 digits rather than 3 digits of precision?
>
> Well, yes, but there is a subtly.  Here you have numbers like 0.12 -- since there's nothing to the left of the decimal you have two digits of precision to the right.  But if everything in the column is shown with the same width, then other numbers will have to go from 4.2 to 4.21.

I agree that it's not a very well defined problem.

Here's what R does, which I also don't understand:

 > print(1.23,digits=2)
[1] 1.2

 > print(c(0.981,1.23),digits=2)
[1] 0.98 1.23

 > print(c(0.00001,1.234567),digits=2)
[1] 0.00001 1.23457

My main concerns are that the scientific notation is
hard to read and that the command-line and R should
be doing something similar.  (Though as I just said, I'm
not even sure what R's doing!)

The more I think about it, the more I like the scientific
notation's ability to keep everything lined up with the
same number of digits.

The real problem is that the columns aren't coherent in what
we're printing --- they can be on all different scales from
the log probability (huge negative) down to small hierarchical
variances.

>> Is the stepsize sd just because there are four chains?
>
> Yup.
>
>> Can we change n_eff/time to n_eff/s?  That does seem to be the unit.
>
> Sure.  I originally wanted "neff/time (samples/s)" but that was way too verbose.

Thanks.  I created an issue.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The way it was set up previously (in circular branch) is to restrict y
and mu to (-pi,pi), so should I change this to [0,2pi) or leave it as is?

On 6/22/13 11:14 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On 6/21/13 11:56 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> There is an ancient branch called circular where somebody implemented
>> a couple of things.
>
> I think the issue there was that we needed tests and doc.
> The implementations looked OK to me the last time I looked.
> So you should definitely start from there, Peter.
>
>> As I recall, there was a
>> question as to whether to go with the convention that the circular
>> distributions be defined on (0,2 * pi) or (-pi,pi). I
>> think it would be best to follow the conventions of the circular R
>> package(s) whatever those are.
>
> Here's the doc for circular:
>
>    http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/circular/circular.pdf
>
> This package is hugely flexible and lets the user define
> the units.  e.g.,
>
>   x <- rvonmises(n=100, mu=circular(0), kappa=1)
>
> where the circular() class is highly configurable.  The default
> is angle in radians, working modularly, so it's not constrained
> to (0, 2*pi) or (-pi, pi) or whatever.
>
> The nice part about working modulo 2*pi is that you get
> 2*pi == 0 instead of a discontinuity.
>
> Even if we restrict the support of von_mises() to [0,2*pi),
> we'll have an option to implement as:
>
>   parameters {
>     real<lower=0, upper=2 * pi()> theta;
>   }
>   model {
>     theta ~ von_mises(kappa);
>   }
>
> or:
>
>   parameters {
>     real theta_raw;
>   }
>   transformed parameters {
>     real<lower=0,upper=2 * pi()> theta;
>     theta <- mod(theta_raw, 2 * pi());
>   }
>   model {
>     theta ~ von_mises(kappa);
>   }
>
> Alternatively, we could have a new data type called "angle".
> It could underlyingly be implemented one of the above two
> ways.
>
> - Bob
>

have an unconstrained varialbe that you took mod 2 * pi so that
it could circle around continuously rather than having 2 * pi
at the opposite end of a line from 0.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] circular distribution mod 2 * pi ?
messages.body_plain:
I think it would be much better to have von_mises(kappa) defined on the whole line (mod 2pi) than restrict it's input to [0,2pi).  The (unconstrained) representation of real<lower=0,upper=2*pi> ends up (potentially) having an unnecessary multi-modality when the mode is anywhere near the end points.  This is going to make sampling much harder than it needs to be for no good reason that I can see.

Cheers,
Marcus
