messages.body_plain:
>> Metropolis acceptance probability.
>
> For what?  NUTS doesn't just generate a proposal then Metropolis
> accept/reject.

Right.  It's the average acceptance probability of all points in the NUTS slice.

> I know.  It's also used in the other packages.
>
> I just thought that this would be the time to change it.
> In the same spirit as changing "burnin" to "warmup",
> we could change "thin" to "keep" or something similar.

If Stan becomes ubiquitous we really could change a ton of vocabulary.  Such power, such responsibility.  :-)

> I agree that it's not a very well defined problem.
>
> Here's what R does, which I also don't understand:
>
> > print(1.23,digits=2)
> [1] 1.2
>
> > print(c(0.981,1.23),digits=2)
> [1] 0.98 1.23
>
> > print(c(0.00001,1.234567),digits=2)
> [1] 0.00001 1.23457
>
> My main concerns are that the scientific notation is
> hard to read and that the command-line and R should
> be doing something similar.  (Though as I just said, I'm
> not even sure what R's doing!)
>
> The more I think about it, the more I like the scientific
> notation's ability to keep everything lined up with the
> same number of digits.
>
> The real problem is that the columns aren't coherent in what
> we're printing --- they can be on all different scales from
> the log probability (huge negative) down to small hierarchical
> variances.

Definitely, and because of that I don't think we can get away from scientific notation.

Here's what we do right now.  The precision sets the number of digits to show, and for each column we scan through the values to see the number of digits that would have to be printed to achieve that precision (a precision of 2 for 0.000012 six additional characters, for example) to determine the max number of printed digits.  If that's too large we switch to scientific notation, otherwise we print in fixed.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] another failure on develop
messages.body_plain:
Ok. I found the reason it isn't working. For anyone that doesn't care about this stuff, you can check out now. It works fine under Windows.

We need to define a static pattern rule. The issue is that the target has no extension. For example, if the Stan file is normal.stan, then the make target in !win is normal.

The target we defined is:
.PRECIOUS: %.cpp %.o
%$(EXE): %.o bin/libstan.a
	@echo ''
	@echo '--- Linking C++ model ---'
	$(LINK.c) -O$O $(OUTPUT_OPTION) $< $(LDLIBS)

Unfortunately, when $(EXE) is empty, this essentially matches every make target, so make chooses not to use it. It uses the default implicit target instead, which uses $(LINK.cxx), I think. I think by updating the make targets, I might be able to fix this once and for all.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
I noticed that in the distribution testing framework, cdfs (and now

variable, y, but log prob doesn't. Is there a reason for this?

Peter

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Testing Distributions
messages.body_plain:
On Jun 28, 2013, at 11:50 AM, Peter Li wrote:
> I noticed that in the distribution testing framework, cdfs (and now cdf_log and ccdf_log) test the lower bound/upper bound of the random variable, y, but log prob doesn't. Is there a reason for this?

Yes, I couldn't reason around what we consider upper and lower bounds. If we take the normal_log(y, mu, sigma) as an example, we can push in {-inf, +inf} for y and mu and expect the result to be -Inf (well -- off by constants, I guess), but what about sigma? If we push in sigma = {0, Inf} do we expect -Inf? Does this hold in general? How do we encode in the tests the lower and upper bounds for every parameter? (I guess I did it for the cdf's, so maybe it's not that difficult.)

We could always test just the first argument, y.

Feel free to change the tests. I built them a while ago and haven't really gone back to update them.

Daniel

>> 1. Vectorize the implementation of the transforms. >> As is, they're just iterating, so a vector of positive >> parameters (as in that compound K-distribution formulation) >> is going to be dog slow. >> > By vectorize, do you mean checking to make sure the length of the vectors are all the same or one and then use vector > operations to carryout the transform? I meant the efficient thing for derivatives -- define a new vari type (for reverse mode) for the Jacobian determinant. This should be easy for the simple lower and upper bound constraints, but more involved for ordered vectors, unit-length vectors, and simplexes, and for covariance and correlation matrices. The implementation should look something like that of the distributions, as there may be vector inputs, but there's only a single return. If you can do more efficient implementations for forward-mode, that'd be good, too. In fact, if you use OperandsAndPartials, you should be able to do both at the same time the way the distributions are being done now. - Bob
